overview: This period shows four genuinely new directions consolidating fast: vision robustness under domain shift, robot manipulation and humanoid control, autonomous navigation/planning, and software-engineering agents. The strongest acceleration is in robot manipulation/humanoids and GPU inference systems, with inference research shifting from generic throughput work toward serving-specific bottlenecks like MoE imbalance, long-context KV management, and diffusion/parallel decode schedules. LLM reliability/audit remains large but is more mature and benchmark-heavy than last period, while agent security stays steady rather than breaking out. One prior prominent direction, robot VLA adaptation, has dropped out, suggesting the field is moving from adapting foundation policies toward narrower control/manipulation primitives and benchmarking real execution failures.

clusters.label: bimanual and humanoid manipulation
clusters.one_line: Learning manipulation and loco-manipulation policies for humanoids and dexterous robots from sparse demonstrations, human video, and multimodal feedback.
clusters.existing_landscape: Tesla Optimus, Figure, Apptronik, Agility Robotics, Sanctuary AI, and Boston Dynamics are the obvious industrial references, but most shipping systems are still teleoperated, task-specific, or heavily scripted. Open-source and research stacks include ROS 2, Isaac Lab/Isaac Gym, MuJoCo, LeRobot, and Open X-Embodiment, but these are not end-to-end products for sparse-demo humanoid skill learning.
clusters.research_industry_gap: Research is now showing that humanoid and bimanual policies can be learned from sparse demonstrations, monocular human video, and mixed vision-touch-language signals, plus self-supervised relabeling and diffusion-guided augmentation for trajectory generation. Industry deployments still depend on hand-engineered motion libraries, teleop, and narrow task routines; they do not expose a product that can take a few clips or demonstrations and produce robust whole-body control policies that generalize across object poses, force regimes, and locomotion-manipulation transitions.
clusters.startup_thesis: Build a humanoid skill acquisition stack for factories and labs: the first product is a teaching system that ingests a handful of teleop sessions and human videos, then outputs deployable whole-body policies for specific repetitive tasks like tote handling, machine tending, bin picking, and inspection pickup. The buyer is a robotics OEM or an industrial integrator that needs to get one humanoid cell into production faster than building a large imitation dataset. Defensibility comes from a proprietary motion-and-contact dataset, failure-labeled trajectories, and closed-loop fine-tuning on real hardware where simulation gaps are large. The wedge should be a task-authoring and policy-validation tool, not a general robotics platform.
clusters.why_now: This cluster is new and large, and its centroid papers are all from the last six weeks. The notable shift is away from generic robot learning toward whole-body control, multimodal motion mimicking, and learning from human video, which is the first credible path to scaling humanoids beyond teleop.
clusters.risks: Humanoid OEMs can absorb this vertically, and the market may stay too small until hardware reliability improves. Real-world contact dynamics, safety certification, and data collection cost are all hard; a startup can easily end up as a services layer for one robot vendor.

clusters.label: GPU inference serving
clusters.one_line: Inference systems for large models that optimize decoding, KV-cache management, expert routing, and multi-GPU utilization.
clusters.existing_landscape: NVIDIA Triton, TensorRT-LLM, vLLM, SGLang, Ray Serve, KServe, and AWS/GCP/Azure managed endpoints already serve generic LLM inference. These stacks are strong on baseline serving but only partially address specialized workloads like diffusion LLM decoding, MoE imbalance, and long-context memory pressure.
clusters.research_industry_gap: The research is moving from generic batching and kernel fusion toward workload-specific serving controls: elastic decoding for diffusion LLMs, removing non-scalable overheads beyond Amdahl limits, CPU-resident KV-cache budgeting, expert binning for MoE skew, and compute-communication overlap for multi-GPU workloads. Current products largely expose static knobs and general-purpose schedulers; they do not give operators first-class control over per-workload decode granularity, expert placement under hardware variability, or memory/latency tradeoffs for mixed long-context and MoE traffic.
clusters.startup_thesis: Ship a serving controller for model operators running heterogeneous inference fleets. The first product is a drop-in control plane that profiles each model/workload, then automatically chooses decoding schedule, KV residency policy, expert placement, and parallelism degree to maximize tokens per dollar under latency SLOs. The buyer is a model-serving team at an AI SaaS company or enterprise running self-hosted models. Defensibility comes from runtime traces, workload fingerprints, and a growing library of optimization policies tuned to real traffic patterns; the hard part is not the kernel, but the closed-loop policy that sits above it.
clusters.why_now: This cluster is growing and the paper set is increasingly specialized, not generic. The new results show practical optimization levers that existing serving stacks treat as implementation details, which makes a control-plane product newly plausible.
clusters.risks: NVIDIA and hyperscalers can fold these optimizations into their stacks, especially the parts that are purely scheduling or memory management. Kernel-level gains commoditize quickly, so the startup needs a broad workload footprint and a real deployment path to avoid becoming a consulting project.

clusters.label: safe autonomous navigation planning
clusters.one_line: Trajectory planning and active perception for UAVs, autonomous vehicles, and surface vehicles under uncertainty and safety constraints.
clusters.existing_landscape: Waymo, Cruise, Aurora, Mobileye, and DJI are the main industrial references on the vehicle and drone sides; Auterion, Skydio, and PX4 cover parts of the UAV stack. Open-source and research tooling includes CARLA, AirSim, ROS navigation stacks, and PX4/ArduPilot, but those are not products that directly expose uncertainty-aware planning with benchmarkable safety guarantees.
clusters.research_industry_gap: Research is converging on planners that explicitly reason about frontier information, uncertainty, field-of-view limits, occlusion risk, and segmentation-aware safety, while industry products still rely on conservative heuristics, hand-tuned maps, and offline validation. The gap is not basic trajectory generation; it is closed-loop planning under partial observability with an active perception objective that can be tuned and audited like a software system.
clusters.startup_thesis: Build a safety-critical navigation planner for commercial drones and slow autonomy programs. The first product is a drop-in planning module that takes obstacle maps, perception confidence, and mission goals, then outputs trajectories with explicit risk scores and fallback behavior for inspection, warehouse, and outdoor flight. The buyer is a UAV OEM or an industrial autonomy team that needs better mission completion without rewriting the flight stack. Defensibility comes from flight logs, failure cases, and a planner that is continuously recalibrated on customer environments, which are hard to synthesize well.
clusters.why_now: This cluster is new and sizable, with multiple papers on frontier-aware MPC, FOV-constrained planning, and safety-aware navigation published within weeks. The research signal is that planning is shifting from reactive control to explicit uncertainty and active perception.
clusters.risks: The market is fragmented and many customers will prefer vertically integrated autonomy from DJI-like incumbents. Regulatory and liability constraints slow adoption, and the same research ideas can be absorbed into existing autopilot and autonomy stacks.

clusters.label: coding-agent governance and evaluation
clusters.one_line: Process-level evaluation, traceability, and governance for agentic software engineering tools.
clusters.existing_landscape: GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Windsurf, JetBrains AI, Amazon Q Developer, and Google Gemini Code Assist already sell coding assistance. Open-source eval stacks like SWE-bench, Devin-style demos, and internal agent observability tools exist, but there is no dominant product for governance, traceability, and process-failure analysis of coding agents.
clusters.research_industry_gap: Research is no longer focused only on whether agents can produce correct code; it is showing that first-try reliability depends more on reasoning effort than tool access, that simulated benchmarks overstate real developer behavior, and that process-level defects and control preservation matter. Shipping products still optimize for speed and autocomplete; they do not expose audit trails, governance conversion, or root-cause analysis of why an agent made a bad edit, skipped a test, or violated a repository policy.
clusters.startup_thesis: Build an agent governance layer for engineering teams using coding assistants at scale. The first product is an observability and policy engine that records agent trajectories, flags process defects, explains failed changes, and enforces repository-specific controls around tests, approvals, and unsafe refactors. The buyer is an engineering org that wants to allow AI coding tools without losing release discipline, especially regulated or scientific software teams. Defensibility comes from proprietary process telemetry, policy templates, and integrations into CI/CD and IDE workflows that incumbents treat as secondary features.
clusters.why_now: This cluster is new and fast-growing, and the representative papers are unusually practical: real IDE interaction logs, repository trajectories, and evidence that benchmark scores miss process failures. That makes the gap between demo-grade coding agents and governable production use much clearer than last quarter.
clusters.risks: Copilot, Cursor, and cloud IDE vendors can add telemetry and policy checks quickly. The buyer may see this as a feature, not a standalone budget, unless the product proves it reduces incident risk or compliance overhead.

clusters.label: cross-domain vision robustness
clusters.one_line: Few-shot anomaly detection, synthetic-image detection, and segmentation under domain shift using foundation models and modality-specific adaptation.
clusters.existing_landscape: OpenAI, Google, and the major cloud providers ship generic vision APIs, and security vendors offer some synthetic-media detection, but there are few dedicated products for robust cross-domain image detection or few-shot anomaly detection in specialized industrial imaging. In practice, companies stitch together Detectron2, MMDetection, Ultralytics, Segment Anything, and custom model pipelines.
clusters.research_industry_gap: Research is finding that foundation vision models can be regularized, calibrated, and decomposed to survive cross-domain shifts in synthetic-to-real segmentation, low-light detection, and AI-generated image detection, including zero-shot and training-free remote-sensing grounding. Shipping products usually assume in-domain training data and fixed capture conditions; they do not expose a robust, continuously adapting detector for sensor drift, synthetic-media provenance, or low-data industrial inspection.
clusters.startup_thesis: Build a robustness layer for industrial and media imaging teams. The first product is an evaluation-and-deployment service that benchmarks a customer’s detector across domains, then supplies calibrated adapters and provenance checks for specific cameras, lighting conditions, and synthetic content sources. The buyer is an industrial QA team, a remote-sensing operator, or a trust-and-safety group screening generated images. Defensibility comes from domain-shift datasets, failure corpora, and calibration/adaptation recipes that are hard to recreate without the same data coverage.
clusters.why_now: This is a large new cluster and the representative papers emphasize domain shift rather than benchmark chasing. The combination of few-shot anomaly detection, synthetic-image detection, and training-free grounding suggests the field is consolidating around practical robustness, not new architectures.
clusters.risks: The market is fragmented across inspection, security, and geospatial use cases, so go-to-market can get narrow quickly. Foundation model vendors could package some of this as a feature, and many buyers may prefer custom integration over standalone software.

clusters.label: neuro-symbolic constrained networks
clusters.one_line: Neural architectures that embed convex, combinatorial, or higher-order structural constraints directly into training and inference.
clusters.existing_landscape: There are research libraries and some niche industrial use of CVXPY, Pyomo, OptNet-style layers, Deep Graph Library, PyTorch Geometric, and differentiable optimization toolkits, but no major dedicated products to my knowledge. Most commercial ML stacks still treat constraints as post-processing or optimization layers outside the core model.
clusters.research_industry_gap: Research here is pushing beyond loose regularization toward hard mixed-integer and convexified constraints inside the network, plus representational analyses that identify non-monotonic task information across layers. Industry tools generally cannot natively express decision constraints, higher-order structure, or layer-selection principles as part of model design; they require bespoke research teams to hand-wire these properties.
clusters.startup_thesis: Build a constrained-model toolkit for regulated and high-stakes optimization teams. The first product is a library and compiler that lets users specify hard constraints, graph structure, or task partitions and then trains models that respect them while remaining deployable in PyTorch/JAX. The buyer is a team working on sensor networks, operations research, or scientific ML where violations are costly. Defensibility comes from a constraint compiler, verified optimization backends, and domain-specific templates that reduce the need for bespoke research.
clusters.why_now: This cluster is new, but the immediate commercial signal is weaker than the robotics and inference clusters. The research is getting more concrete by tying constraint enforcement to trainable layers and scalable graph learning, which improves technical viability.
clusters.risks: This can remain an academic niche if the tooling is too hard to use. Existing ML frameworks and differentiable optimization libraries may absorb the useful pieces, leaving little standalone value.

dropped_clusters.one_line: Adaptation, robustness, and reasoning upgrades for vision-language-action policies in robotics.
